knowledge_type_note: An umbrella record. The middlegame has no compact principle set of its own, and saying so is part of the content.

attributions.note: The accumulation theory is the closest thing the middlegame has to a governing principle: when to attack and why.

history.notes: No single tradition; the middlegame literature is organised by structure and by example rather than by principle.

engine_era_note: The phase engines changed least in principle and most in practice. There is still no compact rule set, but engine analysis has made it possible to check individual judgements, which is what most of this base's measurements are.

false_positive_traps: The phase boundaries are not sharp, and a queenless position with many pieces is still a middlegame. Treating it as an endgame is how kings get mated.
This is an umbrella record. Attaching it to a move explains nothing; the specific concept under it is what carries content.

typical_plans: Assess, then plan from the assessment rather than from preference
Ask what the opponent intends before pursuing your own idea
Improve the worst-placed piece when nothing is urgent
Act once an advantage is sufficient, since it otherwise dissipates
typical_pawn_structures: The structure decides which plans exist, which is why structures are studied rather than positions
strategic_consequences: Small advantages accumulate here and are converted in the endgame

exceptions: Sharp theoretical positions are played from preparation rather than from principle.
Forcing positions require calculation and the procedure above does not apply.
limitations: Deliberately an umbrella; the content is on the concepts it points at.
This is the phase where this base's coverage is broadest and its confidence lowest.
misconceptions: That the middlegame has principles like the opening does. It has a procedure, and the general rules are exactly what have run out by then.
That a plan should be found before the position is assessed. The plan is supposed to follow from the assessment.

examples.note: Rubinstein-Salwe, Lodz 1908, 20.e3 - one quiet pawn move doing four things, which is what a middlegame principle is for. The corpus annotation lists them: 'it gains a tempo by attacking Black's queen, opens a diagonal for the bishop, and improves the worst-placed piece.' This base already files the same move under `worst-placed-piece`, and it is filed here because the record's subject is the ORDER of middlegame thinking - improve the worst piece when nothing is forcing - and this is the move that shows the precondition and the rule together rather than the rule alone.

engine.verdict_note: +0.34, and the engine's own first move is 20.e3. A third of a pawn: the move is best and it is not decisive, which is the correct size for a principle about accumulating rather than about winning.

by_level.beginner: Once your pieces are out, there is no rule to follow — look at the position and find something to aim at.
by_level.intermediate: Assess, plan from the assessment, check what your opponent wants, and improve your worst piece when nothing is urgent.
by_level.advanced: Steinitz's condition governs timing: do not attack without an advantage, and do act once you have one, because it dissipates.
by_level.master: There is no short list because the position differs every game, which is also why this is where the clock goes.

by_depth.short: The phase where you have to judge rather than follow rules.
by_depth.normal: The middlegame has no compact set of principles, because unlike the opening the position differs every game and unlike the endgame it cannot be solved. What replaces them is a procedure: assess, plan from the assessment, watch the opponent's plan, improve the worst piece, and calculate before committing.
by_depth.deep: The absence of a short list is a fact about the phase rather than a gap. The opening has principles because the starting position is always the same; the endgame has principles and, where it does not, tablebases; the middlegame has neither. What replaces them is a procedure whose every step is a concept in its own right, governed by Steinitz's condition on timing - do not attack without an advantage, and do act once you have one, since it otherwise dissipates. It is also measurably the expensive phase: options grow roughly linearly for twenty moves, and strong players spend less time on openings and endings precisely to spend more here.

explanations.hedge: An umbrella over a procedure rather than a rule set; the middlegame is where this base's coverage is broadest and its confidence lowest.
explanations.lesson: There is no rule to follow here. Assess first, and let the plan come from the assessment.

definition_short: The phase where development is finished and the position must be judged and acted on rather than followed.
definition_long:
THE MIDDLEGAME HAS NO SHORT LIST, and that is a fact about it rather than a gap here. The opening has principles because the starting position is the same every time. The endgame has principles, and where it does not it has tablebases. The middlegame has neither: it is the phase in which the position is different every game and the general rules have run out.

WHAT REPLACES THEM IS A PROCEDURE, and every part of it is a concept in its own right here: ASSESS the position by its elements, form a PLAN that the assessment actually points at, check the opponent's plan (PROPHYLAXIS), improve the WORST-PLACED PIECE when nothing is urgent, and CALCULATE the forcing lines before committing.

STEINITZ'S CONDITION governs when to act: do not attack without an advantage, because an attack on a balanced position should fail against correct defence and leave the attacker worse for trying — and conversely, once a sufficient advantage exists it MUST be acted on or it dissipates. Lasker put the same thing from the tactical side: no combination without a considerable plus, and no considerable plus without a combination.

THE MEASURED FACT ABOUT THE PHASE, from this base's practical research, is that the middlegame is where strong players spend their clock. Options grow roughly linearly for the first twenty moves, and players above 1900 spend LESS time than weaker ones on openings and endings in order to spend more here. The phase is expensive because the decisions are genuinely harder, and that is measurable rather than impressionistic.

THIS IS ALSO WHERE THIS SYSTEM HAS THE MOST TO OFFER AND THE LEAST CERTAINTY. The shipped explanation layer names a motif in 65% of tactical puzzles and manages 4% on positional ones; the gap is almost entirely middlegame judgement.
